Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Agribusiness Jospong subsidiary partners Turkish firm to test shrimp-shell-based farm products in Ghana 21 November 2026 11:59pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The African Agribusiness Consortium Limited (AAC), a subsidiary of the Jospong Group of Companies, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Türkiye-based ChitoGlobal Biotechnology to test agricultural products derived from discarded shrimp and crab shells on farms in Ghana.
Signed on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, the agreement will begin with joint research and field trials to assess the products' suitability for Ghanaian farming conditions.
The products are based on chitosan, a substance derived from chitin, which is naturally found in the shells of crustaceans.
The trials will examine whether the products can protect seeds and plants, improve crop resilience during dry spells and strengthen plants' natural defences against fungal diseases.
They will also assess the products' effects on soil quality and crop yields, as well as their potential to provide farmers with a more affordable alternative to some conventional agricultural inputs.
After the signing, Jospong Group Chief Investment and Innovation Officer Noah Gyimah said the company would work with Ghana's environmental and standards authorities to ensure the products meet local regulatory requirements before introducing them for use on its farms.
“Our joint efforts will transition this technology from research and development to practical application. We will commence with collaborative research and field trials in Ghana, followed by technology transfer and full-scale commercial production,” he said.
Mr Gyimah said the pilot would also help AAC assess the commercial viability of the products, identify potential buyers and determine whether Ghana has sufficient raw materials to support local production.
He said the consortium intends to make the products available to smallholder farmers if the trials establish their suitability. AAC also plans to assess their potential use in growing its own crops and vegetables on a commercial scale for the Ghanaian market.
The agreement followed a visit by a four-member AAC delegation, led by the consortium's Coordinator, Dr Emmanuel Volsuuri, to ChitoGlobal's facility in Antalya.
Dr Volsuuri said he arranged the visit after meeting the company at its COP31 pavilion, where further discussions led to the opportunity to examine its operations and technology first-hand.
The delegation toured the facility to learn about the composition of the products and the operations of the company's laboratories.
Dr Volsuuri said the visit helped AAC assess the products' potential to support crop disease management and improve soil health in Ghana.
He also cited concerns about the widespread use of conventional chemical treatments in agriculture and the need to explore alternatives that could reduce farmers' reliance on them.
AAC Chief Executive, Dr Adelaide Araba Siaw Agyepong, leads the consortium, which grows rice, maize, vegetables and soybeans commercially in Ghana. The company also supports farmers with access to mechanisation services, financing and markets.
ChitoGlobal Biotechnology develops biopolymer products for agricultural and medical applications.
ChitoGlobal Sales and Technical Support Manager, Dana Abourahma, said the partnership would combine the expertise of both organisations.
“This collaboration brings together extensive local knowledge with cutting-edge scientific capabilities,” she said.
The proposed research and field trials will determine whether the chitosan-based products can be adapted for Ghanaian farms and whether local production could be commercially viable.
